title: Record Volatility, Resilient Liquidity: What the September/October Bond Sell-Off Reveals About Rates Market Structure
summary: Tradeweb data shows how liquidity held up better relative to volatility than in past rate shocks, a sign of how much market structure has changed.
body_markdown:
*Data analysis by Mihir Chinai, U.S. Institutional Rates Data Science, Tradeweb*


#### **** *Tradeweb data shows how liquidity held up better relative to volatility than in past rate shocks, a sign of how much market structure has changed.*


- **Key Rates Benchmarks Hit Historic High Yields:** The 10-year US Treasury yield closed above 5.0% for the first time in 19 years in September 2026 then climbed further to a 24-year high of 5.3% in early October. Meanwhile, German Bunds hit a 17-year high of 3.6% in September, before falling slightly in October, and UK Gilt yields climbed steadily throughout September, reaching a 19-year high of 5.5% on October 8.


- **Trading Volumes Surge:** Average daily trading volume (ADV) in institutional US Treasuries on Tradeweb was up 33% year-over-year (YoY) in September and 34% YoY in October. In Europe, government bond trading volumes on Tradeweb saw the busiest single month on record in September, with European government bond and UK Gilt ADV both up 30% YoY. European government bond volumes were up 28% YoY in October, while Gilt volumes slowed 13% YoY.


- **Liquidity, Spreads, Quoting Hold Tight:** By all conventional measures of institutional market behavior, including trading costs, bid-offer spreads and dealer quote rates, the September/October bond market sell-off created significantly less disruption than previous periods of heightened volatility.


The last two months have brought some historic moves in rates markets. Before September of this year, the last time 10-year US Treasury yields reached the 5.2% mark was June of 2007. It was the moment when the first cracks were starting to emerge in the subprime mortgage market, two Bear Stearns structured credit funds were collapsing, and we were headed for the worst liquidity crunch in modern history. This year, that 5.2% threshold for the 10-year US Treasury yield was hit first on September 28, and yields continued to climb into early October.


Thankfully, market conditions are very different today, but those differences are bigger than just the macroeconomic backdrop. The underlying structure of rates markets has changed so dramatically that market participants are digesting historic surges in volatility far more efficiently than ever before.


To better understand how institutional rates markets are responding to increased volatility, we’ve analyzed trading activity on the Tradeweb platform to track key trends in trading volumes, liquidity and overall market efficiency throughout the months of September and October 2026. These results were then benchmarked against other recent market stress events, including the February/March 2026 start of the conflict in Iran, the April 2025 “Liberation Day” tariff announcements, the March 2023 Silicon Valley Bank collapse and the COVD-19 pandemic. The conclusion: Institutional markets are getting much better at managing volatility.


#### Historic Yield Moves, Record Volumes


While 10-year government bond yields had been climbing steadily throughout the summer of 2026, the dramatic moves in September and October were notable. Over the course of September, the US 10-year Treasury yield rose 54 basis points (bps). The trend continued into early October, with the 10-year US Treasury yield reaching a 24-year high of 5.3% on October 5. Across Europe, every 10-year benchmark yield rose in a range between 23 and 67bps throughout September, with the largest moves occurring in France, which closed the month up 64bps at 4.8%. German Bunds hit a 17-year high of 3.6% and UK Gilts soared above the 5.0% mark to reach levels not seen since the late 1990s. In October, French 10-year government bond yields rose another 14bps, closing the month at 5.0%, the highest level since 2002.


Not surprisingly, institutional trading volumes rose sharply amid the increased volatility. ADV in US Treasuries on Tradeweb’s institutional platform was $157 billion (bn) in September, up 4% versus August and up 33% YoY. European government bonds and UK gilts both recorded the busiest single month on record. October volumes were slower on a month-to-month basis but were still considerably higher than year-ago totals. Institutional US Treasury ADV in October rose 34% YoY, while European government bond volumes rose 28% YoY. UK Gilt ADV slowed 13% YoY in October.


####
Liquidity Holds Strong


What is slightly more surprising is the relative sense of calm with which institutional market participants digested these moves. While September and October certainly had their fair share of high-stress days, the core measures of rates market liquidity all held remarkably strong throughout the period, especially when compared to previous periods of heightened volatility.


As the chart below indicates, Tradeweb’s composite bid-offer spread for 10-year government bonds in the US and Germany did not deviate by more than one third of a basis point in September and October versus August 2026. Spreads did widen in October in France, UK, Italy, Spain and Belgium, moving roughly in line with the range of movement we saw in March 2026, the last period of heightened volatility following the start of the US conflict with Iran.


Similarly, the Tradeweb Liquidity Index, which measures average trading cost and cost per unit of intraday volatility as a proxy for overall market liquidity, showed very little impact to trading costs stemming from the increased volatility. On the whole, average cost per unit of volatility in US Treasuries was measured at 0.4 in September and 0.51 in October, which is significantly lower than what we saw following the tariff announcements and more than 5x lower than the impacts measured during the COVID-19 pandemic.


####
Deconstructing the Behavioral Component


Across virtually every measure of market efficiency and liquidity, the fundamentals held throughout September and October. Dealer hit rates, trade completion rates, participation of different investor types all held relatively steady with historical averages despite the increased volatility and surging trading volumes.


One particularly fascinating behavioral indicator during these months was the total share of trades executed on our institutional rates platform using Tradeweb AiEX, our automated intelligent execution trading protocol. In US Treasuries, 65.4% of all institutional trades in September were automated, and in October, 57% were automated across all maturities. Throughout the Eurozone, 75% of all government bond trades were done using Tradeweb AiEX in September and 78% were automated in October, roughly flat with August figures. In the UK, 42.2% of government bond trades were automated in September and 45.2% were automated in October, relatively flat as compared to August. While the US Treasury automation rate eased in October, it remained above its level through most of the past eighteen months, and automation in European government bonds and UK Gilts rose to multi-year highs during the sell-off, where both had fallen during the April 2025 tariff episode, suggesting that institutional market participants have grown increasingly confident using technology to help manage risk through volatile periods.


Early November data suggests the resilience has carried forward. On the day after the US midterm elections, intraday volatility in US Treasuries ran at the upper end of October’s range, yet the Tradeweb Liquidity Index measured cost per unit of volatility at 0.49, in line with October’s 0.51 and below the June through August baseline. Trading costs in USD, EUR and GBP swaps all came in below their October averages. The contrast with the last election cycle is telling: the day after the 2024 presidential election, US Treasury trading costs rose roughly 60% versus the prior month, while the 2026 midterm result passed through the market with no measurable liquidity cost. The initial reaction suggests dealers continued to price risk normally through a politically significant and more volatile session, which raises the natural question of whether that resilience can last.


Will the trend continue? While we cannot predict the future direction of markets, we have observed a consistent trend toward increased market efficiency and fewer instances of strained liquidity following stress events over the past several years. Part of that is attributable to macro market trends and market participants’ belief in the underlying strength of the economy, but a big part of it is also structural. Market participants now have more technology and tools at their disposal and more ways to move risk quickly than ever before, and they are using those tools to navigate complex market moves.
